Digital inkjet

Lowest total cost per label as volume and variable-data complexity increase

Two costs that don’t show up on a spec sheet but belong in the model: printhead life for digital inkjet systems, where head replacement is a periodic maintenance item, and reprints and scan failures, which either technology can cause if durability is mismatched to conditions. Fewer barcode rejects meaningfully reduce true cost per label by cutting rework and chargeback risk. This dynamic is explored further in Arrow’s piece on short-run food label production.

ArrowJet Digital Inkjet Presses for Food Label Production

Arrow Systems manufactures digital inkjet label printing hardware — a commercial food label printer lineup covering food and beverage label scenarios from entry-level to high-durability production.

Three of these presses run on Memjet digital label printing technology. Brands running both food and beverage lines can also see Arrow’s guide to digital printing for beverage labels for format considerations specific to bottles and cans.

ArrowJet Aqua 330R II for water-based pigment food label production

The ArrowJet Aqua 330R II runs on a Memjet DuraCore™ engine with a 12.69″ (322 mm) print width, resolution up to 1600 × 1600 dpi, and speed tiers of 90, 150, and 220 ft/min. It prints water-based pigment CMYK ink and is Swiss Ordinance and Indirect Food Contact Safe certified — a relevant specification for teams evaluating label stock in close proximity to food packaging. Brands should still confirm certification scope against their specific product and container against current regulatory requirements.

ArrowJet UV 330H for washdown, cold-storage, and film-substrate durability

The ArrowJet UV 330H is a true hybrid UV label press combining roll-to-roll and flatbed printing. UV-cured ink forms a hard, chemically resistant film directly off the press, supporting CMYK + White, CMYK + Varnish, and CMYK + White + Varnish configurations for opaque printing on film and foil substrates common in frozen and refrigerated food packaging. Standard UV inks are widely used across food secondary packaging; for labels in close or direct food contact, confirm ink migration compliance with your regulatory team rather than relying on a general technology claim. See Arrow’s UV label printers category page for the full UV ink configuration range.

ArrowJet Eco 330R for smaller food and beverage brands entering in-house production

As a compact roll to roll digital inkjet label printer, the ArrowJet Eco 330R runs on a Memjet DuraFlex® engine at up to 20 m/min and a 324 mm print width, on single-phase power with no air compressor required. For food and beverage brands managing a smaller SKU count, it provides an entry point into in-house digital label production without the capital commitment of a high-throughput press — useful when label revisions need to move faster than a converter’s typical turnaround.

ArrowJet Aqua 800M for flexible food packaging formats

For food brands running pouches, sachets, and stick packs alongside roll labels, the ArrowJet Aqua 800M is built for wide-web flexible substrate printing with a high-durability pigmented aqueous inkjet platform. It is a separate press from the label-focused Aqua 330R II and Eco 330R, intended for teams whose food packaging portfolio extends beyond pressure-sensitive labels into flexible film formats.

All four presses print on demand — no plates, no minimum order quantities — which addresses the variable-data and traceability pressure covered above without carrying pre-printed label inventory that becomes obsolete when a lot code, sell-by date, or FSMA 204 recordkeeping field changes.

Arrow Label Finishers for Food Label Die-Cutting and Lamination

Arrow’s EZCut blade die cutters and ArrowCut Nova laser finishers handle die-cutting, lamination, and custom shapes on ArrowJet-printed food label rolls.

Why finishing compatibility matters in food label production

The press is only half the production system. Whether you print on the Aqua 330R II or UV 330H, finishing determines the final label that ships: laminated or not, die-cut to shape, slit, and rewound. Arrow’s full range of label finishing systems keeps the downstream workflow consistent regardless of which press produced the roll.

Arrow EZCut 330R+ — flatbed and roll-to-roll blade die cutting

The EZCut 330R+ is a flatbed and roll-to-roll hybrid blade die cutter with a maximum cutting width of 350 mm, cutting accuracy of ±0.1 mm, and a maximum speed of 150 cuts per minute. It supports self-adhesive, PP synthetic, PET, PVC, and flexible materials — covering the substrate range printed on either the Aqua 330R II or UV 330H. Cold lamination is available inline for washdown or cold-storage SKUs requiring an added protective layer.

Arrow EZCut 350R — higher-throughput multi-blade roll-to-roll cutting

The EZCut 350R is a dedicated roll-to-roll multi-blade cutter with up to 6 cutting heads, a cutting speed of 9 m/min, slitting speed up to 100 m/min, and die cutting precision of ±0.1 mm across a maximum label width of 330 mm. Where the 330R+ suits mixed roll and flatbed jobs, the 350R is built for higher-throughput, consistent label shapes at volume — a fit for core food SKUs running at scale. Barcode-triggered automatic job changeover supports multi-SKU production runs.

ArrowCut Nova — CO₂ laser finishing for custom shapes

The ArrowCut Nova 330R and ArrowCut Nova 250R are laser label finishers that cut without physical dies, enabling custom shapes, perforations, kiss cuts, and etching. Laser finishing suits short-run or seasonal food SKUs — limited-edition flavors, promotional packaging — where die tooling cost cannot be amortized across the print run.

Connecting print and finish into one workflow

When print and finish share job data with minimal manual handoffs, short-run and high-mix food label production becomes economically viable at a per-SKU level. Fewer touchpoints between artwork approval and finished roll reduce turnaround time — important when frequent lot code and sell-by date changes are already compressing the production schedule.

How to Decide: A Practical Framework for Food Packaging Teams

Map your SKU mix, define cold-chain and durability requirements, model total cost across run lengths, and pilot on real substrates before standardizing across the line.

Step 1: Map your SKU mix and exposure environments

List every active and planned SKU. For each one, note substrate, storage environment (ambient, refrigerated, deep-freeze), washdown exposure, and how often the lot code or sell-by date changes. This mapping reveals whether thermal transfer, digital inkjet, or a dual-technology setup best serves the portfolio.

Step 2: Define durability and data-change requirements per cluster

Translate each SKU cluster into specific requirements: freeze/thaw resistance, chemical or caustic exposure, barcode scan thresholds, and how frequently lot codes, sell-by dates, or FSMA 204 recordkeeping fields will change. Requirements should drive the technology choice, not the reverse.

Step 3: Model total cost across run lengths — not just ink or ribbon cost

Include printhead life, ribbon consumption, changeover waste, and scan-failure rework in the comparison. Digital inkjet consistently wins on total cost once revision cycles and SKU proliferation are factored in against pre-printed label inventory.

Step 4: Pilot labels under real cold-chain and washdown conditions

Validate durability before committing the line. Cycle labels through actual freeze/thaw conditions, expose them to real washdown chemicals, and scan barcodes at production line speed. Decisions made on samples that never see the actual storage or handling environment rarely survive real-world deployment. Request label samples from Arrow Systems to pilot on your specific substrates before standardizing.

Frequently Asked Questions — Inkjet vs. Thermal Transfer Food Labels

Common questions from food and beverage packaging, operations, and QA teams evaluating inkjet and thermal transfer for label production.

Which print technology is better for cold chain food labels?

Both can perform in cold chain conditions when matched correctly. Resin thermal transfer on a synthetic substrate is a long-proven combination. Digital inkjet can match it using pigment or UV-cured inks on coated synthetic media — the ArrowJet Aqua 330R II runs water-based pigment ink on synthetic and coated stocks. The deciding factor is chemistry-to-substrate fit and how much your variable data changes.

Do inkjet food labels smear on frozen or condensation-covered packaging?

They can if the ink is not fully dried or applied to an unsuitable substrate. Properly matched digital inkjet systems using pigment inks on coated synthetic stock, with NIR or IR drying support, are designed to resist wet-rub and hold up through condensation and thaw cycles. Testing under your actual cold chain conditions is essential before standardizing on any press.

Which produces more reliable, scannable barcodes at food production line speed?

Both resin thermal transfer and high-resolution digital inkjet can produce retail-grade, scannable barcodes at line speed. Reliability depends on resolution, contrast, and substrate. Inline verification is the best way to catch marginal codes before product ships, regardless of which print technology you choose.

At what run length does digital inkjet become more cost-effective than thermal transfer for food labels?

As an illustrative rule of thumb, thermal transfer often stays competitive for very short, low-variety runs, while digital inkjet typically becomes more economical as SKU variety and volume grow, because it eliminates plate, ribbon, and changeover overhead. Your true break-even depends on substrate, coverage, and consumable costs, so it should be modeled against your specific run profile.

Which ArrowJet press is right for food label printing?

It depends on your substrate mix, durability requirements, and SKU volume. The ArrowJet Aqua 330R II is built for food-contact-adjacent label applications with water-based pigment ink. The ArrowJet UV 330H suits high-durability, washdown, and cold-storage SKUs on film substrates. The ArrowJet Eco 330R is a lower-investment entry point for smaller food and beverage brands moving label production in-house. Arrow Systems sells the hardware; a structured assessment can match a configuration to your SKU mix.

What is the best thermal printer for food labels?

It depends on the SKU. Thermal transfer remains a strong, proven choice for low-SKU, infrequently-changing, high-durability runs — the best thermal printer for food labels is still the right call when barcode scan reliability and freeze/thaw durability matter more than variable-data flexibility. For operations with growing SKU variety, frequent lot code or sell-by date changes, or full-color label requirements, a commercial food label printer using digital inkjet technology typically wins on total cost and flexibility. The best answer comes from mapping your actual SKU mix against both technologies rather than defaulting to whichever one your operation has always used.

title.rendered: Natural Wine Label Printing: Design, Materials & In-House Options

content.rendered:
Table of Contents

Natural Wine Label Printing: Design, Materials & In-House Options

Natural wine labels stand apart through bold illustration, farming values, and artistic identity — and small producers can now print custom runs in-house with no plates or minimums.

Natural wine labels are distinctive because independent producers use them to communicate a farming philosophy and artistic identity, not just varietal and appellation. For producers printing in-house, digital inkjet label presses eliminate plate costs and minimum order quantities, making short-run, artwork-driven production practical at any scale.

Key Takeaways

  • Natural wine labels use illustration, collage, photography, and unconventional color — reflecting the independent character of the producers behind them.
  • Wine bottle labels must survive condensation, refrigeration, and ice-bucket conditions — substrate selection and ink technology matter as much as design.
  • UV-cured inkjet printing delivers moisture-resistant output with premium effects (spot varnish, opaque white, multi-layer finishes) that match natural wine label ambitions.
  • Sustainability claims on labels must be accurate and traceable to verified certifications — not used as general marketing language.

Why Natural Wine Labels Stand Out

Natural wine labels are visually distinctive because independent producers use them to communicate who they are, not just what is in the bottle.

Natural wine labels have become almost as recognizable as the bottles themselves. They look different from conventional wine packaging — more playful, more experimental, more personal. That difference is not accidental. It reflects the natural wine movement’s origins as a community built around small growers, unconventional winemaking, and a deliberate departure from mainstream wine aesthetics. Where established wine brands lean on heritage cues — crests, estates, formal typography — natural wine producers reach for illustration, photography, collage, and unexpected color palettes.

The artists behind these labels are as eclectic as the wines: children’s book illustrators, tattoo artists, photographers, and printmakers all work in this space. The result is a category where label art is genuinely unpredictable, and where visual identity has become one of the primary ways producers differentiate on a crowded shelf.

Design Elements That Define the Category

Natural wine label design draws from illustration, collage, and fine art — techniques that signal independence and personality over category convention.

Hand-drawn illustration

Original artwork — whimsical animals, botanical drawings, imagined landscapes, abstract figures — signals a specific human made this wine, not a marketing template. Illustrators in this space frequently bring backgrounds in printmaking, tattooing, or street art.

Collage and mixed media

Cut-paper and photo collage techniques give labels a handmade, layered quality that reads as intentional rather than unfinished — and is difficult to replicate with purely digital design tools.

Creative photography

Documentary portraits, vineyard imagery, and close-up soil or vine photography connect the label directly to a person, a place, or a moment in the growing season.

Unconventional typography

Natural wine labels often break conventional hierarchy — hand-lettered scripts, oversized producer names, or type borrowed from vintage posters and zine culture rather than classical wine fonts.

Unexpected color palettes

Electric blues, deep terracottas, pastels, and combinations that would read as too bold in traditional wine branding. Color is used to signal category departure as much as aesthetic preference.

Farming Values and Label Storytelling

Natural wine labels often carry a farming philosophy directly — sustainability, terroir, and handmade character are all legitimate elements of label storytelling.

Natural wines are associated with organic growing, biodynamic practices, cover cropping, and a focus on soil health through beneficial microbe populations. The movement traces its origins to 1990s Paris and developed in reaction against industrial vineyard management and winemaking additives. Many producers in this space have been farming this way for decades, and their labels reflect it — a hand-drawn vineyard map, soil cross-sections, insect and bird imagery, or simply the personality of the producer in a way that signals authenticity over polish.

Any farming or sustainability claim on a label must be accurate and specific to be credible. Here are the key designations natural wine producers typically reference:

Organic certification (USDA)

Wines must be produced from organically grown grapes, made in a USDA-certified facility, and contain added sulfites below 100 ppm. Active certification must be maintained annually.

Biodynamic farming

A holistic approach treating the vineyard as a self-sustaining ecosystem. Demeter certification is separate from organic certification and involves additional auditing requirements.

Natural wine (working definition)

No universally accepted legal definition exists. Producers generally use native yeast fermentation, minimal or no added sulfur, and avoid the 300-plus additives permissible in conventional wine production.

Label Materials and Ink Technology for Wine Bottles

Wine bottle labels must survive condensation, refrigeration, and ice-bucket conditions — substrate and ink choices are as important as the design itself.

Labels that look compelling in a design file must perform in a very different environment on a retail shelf or restaurant table. Glass bottles accumulate condensation in refrigerated displays and sweat heavily when removed from ice baths. Polypropylene (PP) and BOPP films offer substantially better moisture resistance than paper and maintain adhesion in wet conditions — the standard substrate choice for most wine bottle label applications. UV-cured inkjet printing adds another layer of durability: UV inks deliver vibrant, moisture-resistant color that also supports premium effects including spot varnish, opaque white on metallic stocks, and multi-layer tactile finishes.

The ArrowJet UV 330H is a hybrid UV label press that combines roll-to-roll and flatbed printing in one system, supporting CMYK plus White and CMYK plus Varnish configurations. Food and beverage labels are a confirmed application. These capabilities map directly to the premium visual effects natural wine producers pursue — varnish overlays that make illustration details pop, opaque white under-printing on metallized stocks, and consistent high-resolution output across short runs. Producers evaluating UV label printing can review the full range at ArrowJet UV label printers.

Substrate Options for Wine Bottle Labels

Substrate

Moisture Resistance

Best Application

Pressure-sensitive paper

Low — not suitable for ice-bucket or refrigerated-display exposure

Cellar-direct sales, ambient-temperature tasting room

Polypropylene (PP) film

High — resists condensation and brief water exposure

Refrigerated retail, on-premise/restaurant, general distribution

BOPP film

High — dimensional stability maintained under moisture

Premium wine, export, long-cellaring, ice-bucket service

Coated paper + UV overlaminate

Medium — improved over bare paper, not equivalent to PP

Boutique retail where limited moisture exposure is expected

In-House Label Printing for Natural Wine Producers

Digital label presses let natural wine producers print short runs with no plates, no minimums, and full artwork flexibility — ideal for vintage rotations, limited releases, and artist collaborations.

Many natural wine producers release small batches, rotate artwork by vintage, or collaborate with different artists across individual bottlings. This creative flexibility is extremely difficult to manage through a commercial label printer, where plate costs, minimum order quantities, and lead times make short-run or variable-artwork production expensive and slow. In-house digital label printing removes these friction points. A digital inkjet label press prints from a file — no plates, no makeready — and a single-label proof costs the same in setup time as a full production run.

The ArrowJet Aqua 330R is an aqueous inkjet digital label press built on the Memjet DuraFlex® platform, producing high-resolution output on coated paper, PP, BOPP, PET, Mylar, and other pressure-sensitive substrates across a 330mm web width. Producers printing bottle labels, back labels, and neck labels from the same machine cover their full label format range from a single in-house system. Arrow’s full range of digital label printers covers configurations for wineries from boutique scale to higher-volume operations.

Interested in in-house wine label printing? Arrow Systems offers digital label presses for wineries of all sizes. Request a sample print or contact the team to discuss your production requirements.

Balancing Creativity and Compliance

Natural wine labels can be bold and artistic, but they must still carry required regulatory information — and sustainability claims must be verifiable.

In the United States, wine labels are regulated by the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB). Required elements include brand name, class and type designation, appellation of origin where applicable, alcohol content by volume, net contents, bottler name and address, government health warning, and a sulfite declaration where applicable. Design-forward natural wine labels handle these requirements by treating compliance elements as part of the visual system, not afterthoughts — typography, placement hierarchy, and the front-to-back label relationship all affect how required information integrates with overall identity.

Sustainability claims require particular care. Organic, biodynamic, or certified sustainable designations must reflect actual certifications and production methods — a label should not carry the term “organic” without active USDA certification status. Broader claims like “natural” or “eco-friendly” without substantiation may create exposure under the FTC’s Green Guides on environmental marketing. The most credible natural wine labels are specific: they name a certification or a practice rather than reaching for generic environmental language.

Frequently Asked Questions — Natural Wine Labels

Why are natural wine labels so creative and distinctive?

Natural wine producers use labels to express the individuality of the wine, the grower, and the farming philosophy behind the bottle. Because the category is driven by small, independent producers, artistic freedom is a core part of brand identity — not just the packaging.

What label materials work best for wine bottles?

Polypropylene (PP) and BOPP films offer the best moisture resistance for wine bottle applications, maintaining adhesion through refrigeration, condensation, and ice-bucket conditions. Paper labels are suitable for ambient-temperature retail or cellar-direct settings where moisture exposure is limited.

Can small wine producers print labels in-house?

Yes. Digital label presses allow small wineries to produce runs as low as a single label with no plate costs or minimum order quantities — practical for boutique producers who rotate artwork by vintage or produce small-batch SKUs.

What ink technology is recommended for wine bottle label printing?

UV-cured inkjet inks deliver vibrant, moisture-resistant output suited for wine bottle labels, and support premium effects including spot varnish, opaque white on metallic substrates, and multi-layer tactile finishes. The ArrowJet UV 330H is a hybrid UV label press built for food and beverage label applications.

Should sustainability claims appear on natural wine labels?

Only when accurate and supportable. Claims about organic, biodynamic, or sustainable practices must match actual certifications — USDA organic wines must meet specific production and sulfite standards. Vague terms like “eco-friendly” without substantiation may create exposure under FTC environmental marketing guidelines.

title.rendered: Barcode Label Printing: What They Are, How They Work, and How to Print Them In-House

content.rendered:
Table of Contents

Barcode Label Printing: What They Are, How They Work, and How to Print Them In-House

A barcode label encodes product or tracking information as machine-readable lines or patterns — connecting physical objects to digital systems across retail, logistics, healthcare, and manufacturing.

Barcode labels encode identifying information as a pattern of lines, dots, or squares that a scanner reads in under a second. They are the primary mechanism for connecting a physical product to the inventory, pricing, or traceability system that manages it — across retail, logistics, healthcare, manufacturing, and food supply chains. Arrow Systems’ ArrowJet Aqua 330R and ArrowJet Eco 330R are digital label presses purpose-built for in-house barcode label production. The right press depends on your substrate, volume, and print width requirements.

Key Takeaways

  • Barcode labels give physical objects a machine-readable identity — eliminating manual data entry at checkout, in warehouses, and throughout supply chains.
  • Both 1D barcodes (UPC, Code 128, Code 39) and 2D codes (QR, Data Matrix, GS1-128) are printed on labels — each suited to different data-density and application requirements.
  • Scan reliability depends on print resolution, ink contrast, label substrate, quiet zone margins, and field handling — not just barcode design or symbology choice.
  • Digital label printing equipment allows businesses to produce barcode labels in-house at production volumes, eliminating minimum order requirements and reducing lead times on label artwork changes.
  • The ArrowJet Aqua 330R and ArrowJet Eco 330R are Arrow Systems’ digital label presses for in-house barcode label production — covering high-throughput and entry-level industrial requirements respectively.

From Checkout Problem to Everyday Infrastructure

Barcode labels were created to solve one specific problem — making grocery checkout faster — and grew into the identification backbone of modern commerce, logistics, and healthcare.

Barcode labels are so common today that most people barely notice them. They appear on retail products, shipping cartons, hospital wristbands, library books, airline boarding passes, and thousands of other objects that need to be identified, tracked, or priced. Yet the idea behind them changed the way modern commerce and logistics work.

In the late 1940s, Joe Woodland — an inventor from Ohio vacationing in Miami Beach — began searching for a way to encode product information as a visual pattern that a machine could read. His early work drew on Morse code principles, extending dots and dashes into lines of varying widths. Woodland filed one of the earliest barcode patents in 1949, though the scanning and computing technology required to make the system commercially practical took decades to follow.

The first commercial barcode scanner was deployed at retail checkout in 1974. From that point, standardized label formats and falling scanner costs drove rapid adoption — from grocery stores into manufacturing plants, warehouses, hospitals, airports, and distribution centres worldwide. What began as a checkout solution became foundational infrastructure for the entire modern supply chain.

Why Barcode Labels Became Essential

Barcode labels solve a fundamental operational problem — they give physical objects a machine-readable identity that any compatible scanner can recognise instantly, eliminating manual data entry at every point in the supply chain.

Before barcodes, tracking a product through a warehouse, store, or supply chain relied on manual data entry — slow, error-prone, and expensive to scale. A barcode label removes that manual step entirely. The scanner reads the label; the connected system updates automatically.

In retail, price lookups happen instantly at checkout. In logistics, every package movement is logged without a human typing a tracking number. In healthcare, patient wristbands and medication containers are matched by scan rather than visual inspection. In food manufacturing, a single barcode scan connects a product to its batch record, supplier, and distribution path. The value is consistency at scale: the same information, read the same way, every time — regardless of who is operating the scanner or where in the world the product is moving.

Barcode Label Use Cases Across Industries

Barcode labels are now used in virtually every industry that moves, stores, or dispenses physical goods — from retail and logistics to healthcare, food manufacturing, and pharmaceuticals.

Industry

Barcode Label Application

Common Barcode Format

Retail

Product pricing, point-of-sale scanning, inventory management

UPC-A, EAN-13

Logistics & Shipping

Package tracking, carrier scanning, route sorting

Code 128, GS1-128

Healthcare

Patient identification, medication verification, specimen tracking

Data Matrix, Code 128

Manufacturing

Batch tracking, work-in-progress routing, component identification

Code 39, Data Matrix

Food & Beverage

Lot traceability, expiry date encoding, retailer compliance labelling

GS1 DataBar, GS1-128

Publishing

ISBN encoding on book covers, library cataloguing systems

EAN-13, ITF-14

Pharmaceuticals

Unit-level serialisation, anti-counterfeiting, dispensing verification

Data Matrix, GS1-128

Events & Travel

Ticket validation, boarding passes, access control

QR Code, PDF417

Format selection should be driven by data requirements and scanning infrastructure — not by familiarity with a particular symbology. Validate your format choice against your scanner hardware and any retail or regulatory partner requirements before committing to a label design.

Barcode Label Types and Formats

Barcode labels are now used in virtually every industry that moves, stores, or dispenses physical goods — from retail and logistics to healthcare, food manufacturing, and pharmaceuticals.

1D barcodes (linear barcodes)

Encode data as a series of vertical bars and spaces of varying widths. Read by a single horizontal scan. Common formats include UPC-A (retail consumer products in North America), Code 128 (shipping and logistics), EAN-13 (retail globally), and Code 39 (manufacturing and industrial). Best for product identification, shipping labels, and retail applications where data storage needs are limited.

2D barcodes

Encode data in a two-dimensional grid of squares, dots, or hexagons. Store significantly more information than 1D codes — including URLs, lot numbers, expiry dates, and serialised identifiers — in a smaller printed area. Common formats include QR Code, Data Matrix, and PDF417. Best for healthcare, pharmaceutical serialisation, food traceability, and variable-data applications requiring compact, high-density encoding.

UPC-A (Universal Product Code)

The standardised 1D barcode used on retail consumer products in North America. Encodes 12 numeric digits identifying the product and its manufacturer. The UPC-A is the format most consumers encounter at a retail checkout — it was first deployed commercially in 1974.

GS1-128

A linear barcode standard used in supply chain and logistics. Encodes batch numbers, expiry dates, GTINs, and shipping unit identifiers within a single label using Application Identifiers. Required by many major retailers, distributors, and food manufacturers for case-level and pallet-level labelling compliance.

Data Matrix

A compact 2D barcode format widely used in healthcare, electronics, and aerospace. Encodes large amounts of data in a very small print area — making it suited to small parts, medical devices, pharmaceutical unit-dose packaging, and components where available label real estate is minimal.

QR Code

A 2D barcode capable of storing URLs, text, contact information, or structured data. Originally developed for automotive parts tracking, QR codes are now used across consumer marketing, product authentication, and supply chain traceability applications.

Design and Print Considerations for Barcode Labels

A barcode label must be more than present on a product — it must be reliably readable in the environment where it will actually be used, across the full lifecycle of the product.

Print resolution

Barcode bars must be sharp and dimensionally consistent to scan reliably. A minimum of 300 dpi is generally accepted for 1D barcodes. 2D codes such as Data Matrix typically require 600 dpi or higher to resolve the fine grid structure accurately — particularly at small print sizes where bar width tolerances are tightest.

Ink contrast

Scanners read the contrast ratio between dark bars and light spaces. Low-contrast combinations — dark ink on a dark substrate, or light ink without sufficient opacity — cause scan failures. Dark ink on a white or light-coloured background is the accepted standard for maximum scan reliability across 1D and 2D formats.

Label material and substrate

The substrate affects ink adhesion, surface smoothness, and the sharpness of printed barcode edges. Coated papers, BOPP film, and polyester label stocks produce cleaner bar edges than uncoated or textured materials. Substrate choice also determines whether the label survives the storage, transport, and end-use conditions the product will encounter — moisture, heat, chemicals, or abrasion.

Quiet zones

Every barcode format specification requires clear margins — called quiet zones — on each side of the barcode symbol. These blank areas allow the scanner to locate the start and end of the code. Cropping quiet zones at the print, die-cut, or application stage is one of the most common preventable causes of scan failure in production environments.

Label placement

A correctly printed barcode on the wrong surface or in the wrong position still fails at the scanner. Labels applied to highly curved surfaces, recessed areas, or locations near package seams or folds can distort barcode geometry and reduce scan reliability — regardless of print quality.

Handling and environmental conditions

Labels in cold-chain, outdoor, chemical, or high-traffic environments need materials and inks rated for those conditions. A label that scans correctly off the press but degrades through moisture, abrasion, UV exposure, or chemical contact creates downstream failures in inventory and traceability systems that are difficult to trace back to the label as the root cause.

Printing Barcode Labels In-House

Digital label printing equipment allows businesses to produce barcode labels at production volumes in-house — eliminating minimum order requirements, reducing lead times, and enabling immediate label updates when lot data, regulatory content, or artwork changes.

Outsourcing barcode label production introduces lead times, minimum order quantities, and version control risk on pre-printed stock. When lot information, regulatory content, or SKU details change, pre-printed inventory becomes obsolete. In-house digital label printing eliminates that constraint — each run is printed on demand, exactly to specification, with no minimum volume.

Arrow Systems manufactures digital label printing equipment for in-house label production. Two presses are directly relevant for barcode label production at industrial volumes:

ArrowJet Aqua 330R — high-speed digital pigment inkjet label press

The ArrowJet Aqua 330R uses Memjet’s DuraFlex technology to print at up to 150 ft/min at 1600 × 1600 dpi — producing barcode labels with the resolution and bar-edge sharpness required for reliable scanning across 1D and 2D symbologies. Handles coated papers, BOPP, PET, and other label substrates up to 15″ media width. Available with a 10L bulk ink system for high-volume continuous production runs. Compatible with fully integrated digital finishing for offline or inline configurations.

ArrowJet Eco 330R — compact industrial digital label press

A compact industrial single-pass digital press designed for operations stepping up from desktop printers. Runs on single-phase power and requires no air compressor — reducing installation complexity and operating costs. Prints at up to 20 m/min at 1600 × 1600 dpi on label and flexible packaging substrates up to 324 mm print width. A practical entry point for in-house barcode label production without the footprint or infrastructure requirements of a large press.

Print speed, resolution, and substrate compatibility specifications are sourced from Arrow Systems product documentation. Validate against your specific substrate and barcode symbology requirements before press selection. Arrow Systems sells label printing hardware — Arrow does not provide label design, barcode verification, or compliance advisory services.

The Modern Role of Barcode Labels

Barcode labels are now part of the operating infrastructure of modern commerce, logistics, and healthcare — a functional requirement, not a convenience feature, in any industry that moves or manages physical goods at scale.

They are how supply chains maintain real-time inventory visibility. How retailers reconcile physical stock against digital records. How hospitals verify patient identity and medication matches at the point of care. How food manufacturers trace products from a production batch to a specific retail location when a recall is initiated. The value of any single barcode label is modest. The value of a consistent, system-wide barcode identification standard is enormous.

As regulatory requirements for lot traceability, unit-level serialisation, and supply chain documentation continue to expand — across food and beverage, pharmaceutical, medical device, and consumer product sectors — the demand for accurate, high-resolution barcode labels at scale continues to grow. For businesses in regulated industries, the ability to print correct, compliant barcode labels in-house is becoming an operational requirement, not just a cost optimisation.

Frequently Asked Questions — Barcode Label Printing

Common questions from operations, procurement, and packaging teams evaluating barcode label production for retail, logistics, healthcare, and regulated-industry applications.

What are barcode labels used for?

Barcode labels are used to identify, track, price, and connect physical items to digital records across retail, logistics, healthcare, manufacturing, food and beverage, publishing, and pharmaceutical applications. They are the primary mechanism for connecting a physical product to the inventory, pricing, or traceability system that manages it — at the speed and consistency that manual data entry cannot match.

What is the difference between 1D and 2D barcodes?

A 1D barcode (such as a UPC-A or Code 128) encodes data as a series of vertical bars and is read with a single horizontal scan. A 2D barcode (such as a QR Code or Data Matrix) encodes data in a two-dimensional grid and stores significantly more information — including expiry dates, lot numbers, URLs, and serialised identifiers — in a smaller printed area. The choice between 1D and 2D depends on how much data needs to be encoded and the scanning equipment in use at the destination.

What affects barcode label scan reliability?

Print resolution, ink contrast between bars and background, label substrate surface, quiet zone margins, label placement, and field handling conditions all affect whether a barcode scans reliably. The most common preventable causes of scan failure are insufficient print resolution, low contrast between ink and substrate, and quiet zones cropped during the die-cutting or application process.

Can businesses print their own barcode labels in-house?

Yes. Digital label printing equipment lets businesses produce barcode labels in-house at industrial volumes. Arrow Systems manufactures digital label presses — including the ArrowJet Aqua 330R and ArrowJet Eco 330R — designed for in-house label production. Printing in-house eliminates minimum order requirements, reduces lead times, and allows label artwork to be updated immediately when lot information, regulatory content, or SKU details change.

Why did barcode labels become so widely used?

Barcode labels became widely adopted because they provided a reliable, low-cost method to eliminate manual data entry at checkout, in warehouses, and throughout supply chains. A scanner reading a barcode is faster, more consistent, and less prone to error than manual data recording — and the same label format can be read by any compatible scanner anywhere in the world, making global standardisation viable at scale.

The ArrowJet Aqua 330R handles high-speed production at 150 ft/min and 1600 × 1600 dpi across a wide range of label substrates. The ArrowJet Eco 330R is the compact industrial entry point for operations stepping up from desktop equipment.

title.rendered: Pet Food Label Design: AAFCO Compliance & Printing Guide

content.rendered:
Table of Contents

Pet Food Label Design: AAFCO Compliance & Printing Guide

Pet food labels must satisfy specific AAFCO label requirements — guaranteed analysis, net quantity, and calorie content each have fixed placements.

AAFCO-compliant pet food labels generally require product identity, net quantity, guaranteed analysis, ingredient list, nutritional adequacy statement, feeding directions, calorie content, and manufacturer information. The guaranteed analysis pet food panel belongs on the information panel in tabular format — not the front panel. For brands managing frequent reformulations and multi-SKU portfolios, on-demand digital printing with presses like the ArrowJet Aqua 330R (rigid can and bottle stocks) and ArrowJet Aqua 800M (flexible bags and pouches) eliminates plate costs and shortens revision cycles. Always verify placement and content requirements against current AAFCO model regulations and applicable state rules.

Key Takeaways

  • Treat AAFCO compliance declarations as structural layout inputs from the first wireframe — not artwork added afterward.
  • The guaranteed analysis belongs on the information panel in aligned tabular format, separated from the calorie statement and ingredient list, with space reserved for future guarantees.
  • The principal display panel (PDP) carries two required elements — product identity and net quantity — with net quantity in the lower third, kept clear of imagery.
  • Legibility failures are more common than content failures: small type, low contrast, and condensed typefaces on information panels cause most compliance problems.
  • Functional ingredient claims must be truthful, substantiated, and consistent with the product’s formulation — build them as modular, independently approvable blocks.
  • The ArrowJet Aqua 330R handles cans, jars, and bottles; the ArrowJet Aqua 800M handles flexible packaging up to 638mm; the ArrowJet Eco 330R is the entry-level path into in-house production.

The AAFCO and FDA Framework for Pet Food Label Design

Pet food label design follows FDA expectations and AAFCO label standards, including AAFCO dog food standards, adopted variably by state.

Requirements vary by product type, species, and market, so treat the points below as general guidance to verify against current sources. The compliance challenge isn’t knowing the required elements — it’s placing each one correctly, at legible size, without crowding the brand’s shelf presence.

Product identity

The product name and species statement appear on the principal display panel and set the context for all other declarations.

Net quantity of contents

Appears on the principal display panel, typically lower third, in both U.S. customary and metric units. Decorative elements must not overlap this zone.

Guaranteed analysis

Lists minimum or maximum percentages of crude protein, fat, fiber, and moisture, plus additional guarantees for specific claims. Belongs on the information panel as an aligned table.

Ingredient list

Listed in descending order of pre-processing weight, on the information panel alongside the guaranteed analysis.

Nutritional adequacy statement

States whether the product is complete and balanced for a life stage, or intended for supplemental feeding — wording must match how it was formulated or tested.

Feeding directions

Quantity and frequency guidance for the species and product type, on the information panel.

Calorie content statement

Metabolizable energy per kilogram and per a household measure, on the information panel, separated from the guaranteed analysis.

Manufacturer or distributor information

Name and address of the responsible party. For private label products, confirm who that responsible party is.

Effective AAFCO pet food label design treats compliance as a structural input from the first wireframe, not artwork added afterward.

Guaranteed Analysis: How to Display It Correctly

Guaranteed analysis pet food panels belong on the information panel in tabular format, with room reserved for future claim guarantees.

Panel placement

The guaranteed analysis belongs on the information panel, not the front panel — a common first-time mistake that creates compliance exposure.

Tabular format

Use a tabular or stacked format with each nutrient and percentage aligned in separate rows — easier to scan and audit than running text.

Type legibility

Avoid reversing small numerals out of busy imagery. Test legibility at actual print size on the real substrate, not just on screen.

Building in room to grow

Reserve extra rows for future functional claims (joint support, digestive health). A table built with room to grow absorbs reformulation changes as a file edit, not a layout rebuild.

Dog food vs. cat food panels

Guaranteed analysis dog food panels carry the highest SKU volume for most brands, since dog food is the largest pet food segment. Cat food guaranteed analysis panels follow the same rules but often add taurine and other feline-specific guarantees — confirm species-specific requirements before finalizing either.

Calorie Statement, Net Quantity, and Nutritional Adequacy Placement

Three declarations frequently cause first-submission failures because their placement and wording are specific.

Calorie statement

Expressed as metabolizable energy in kcal per kilogram and per a household measure such as a cup or treat. Give it its own labeled line — “Calorie Content” — separated from the guaranteed analysis.

Net quantity

Belongs on the PDP, lower third, in both U.S. customary and metric units, scaled to package size. One of the most frequently cited placement violations in retailer audits.

Nutritional adequacy statement

Must match how the product was formulated or tested — cannot make a life-stage claim the substantiation method doesn’t support.

The practical fix: map a dedicated “regulatory column” on the information panel where these declarations live in a predictable, repeatable order.

Designing the Principal Display Panel for Pet Food

The PDP must carry product identity and net quantity while leaving room for brand storytelling within those constraints.

Visual hierarchy

Sequence: brand mark, product name and identity, species statement, then net quantity — each visually distinct.

Species statement clarity

Buyers must immediately identify the intended species at arm’s length. Small-type species statements are a top retailer compliance concern.

Net quantity zone

Lower third, with clear space around it — no overlapping badges or decorative elements. Non-negotiable in retailer planogram reviews.

Claim discipline

Keep the front clean; push detail to the information panel. One or two substantiated claims is manageable — four or five degrades legibility.

A worked PDP sequence: top third — brand logo and hero image; middle band — product name and species/intent line with one supporting claim; lower third — net quantity, clear of imagery.

Typography and Color Considerations for Regulatory Text

Compliance text fails most often on legibility, not content — correct data in unreadable type is functionally non-compliant.

Typeface selection

Use a clean, neutral typeface for regulatory blocks. Save display fonts for brand elements.

Contrast

Dark type on a light, solid field outperforms text over imagery or textured backgrounds — a top issue in retailer compliance audits.

Line spacing

Maintain generous spacing in dense blocks so rows and ingredients stay individually scannable, especially on long ingredient lists.

Avoid condensed type

If content doesn’t fit, expand the panel or reduce front-panel clutter — don’t compress type to force a fit.

Substrate selection also shapes legibility: textured, recycled, or specialty facestocks respond differently to fine regulatory text than standard coated paper. Review Arrow’s label substrate range to match facestock to your regulatory text requirements. Minimum type sizes vary by declaration and package size — verify current requirements for your markets.

Handling Functional Ingredient Claims Without Overstating

Functional ingredient claims drive purchase decisions but carry the highest compliance risk in pet food labeling.

Truthfulness and substantiation

Every claim must be truthful, substantiated, and consistent with the formulation — supported by the guaranteed analysis or ingredient list.

Medical implication risk

“Supports joint health” is a structure-function claim; “treats arthritis” is a drug claim. Crossing that line carries significant regulatory consequences.

Modular claim blocks

Build claim text as independent layout blocks so one formula change doesn’t require re-laying the entire label.

Supplement and treat differences

Required elements and adequacy wording can differ from complete-and-balanced foods — confirm the right framework per product type.

Regulatory validation — including AAFCO substantiation and FDA compliance — is the brand’s responsibility. Arrow Systems manufactures printing hardware; Arrow does not provide regulatory or compliance advisory services.

Matching the Press to Your Package Format

On-demand digital printing supports rigid and flexible pet food formats — short runs, fast versioning, and multi-SKU agility.

Pet food portfolios typically span rigid containers (cans, jars, bottles for wet food and supplements) and flexible substrates (bags, pouches, sachets for dry food and treats). Matching equipment to format is the first decision in a digital workflow.

ArrowJet Aqua 330R for Pressure-Sensitive Can and Bottle Labels

Rigid format applications

Wet food, broth, and supplement formats need pressure-sensitive labels that hold fine text through distribution and handling. The ArrowJet Aqua 330R delivers the resolution needed for legible guaranteed analysis tables and dense ingredient lists.

Short runs and fast versioning

For multi-SKU portfolios, digital production eliminates plate costs and minimum order quantities. An updated guaranteed analysis or new claim block becomes a file change, not a plate reorder with weeks of lead time.

ArrowJet Aqua 800M for Flexible Bags and Stand-Up Pouches

Flexible substrate support

The ArrowJet Aqua 800M handles coated paper, PP, PET, PVC, BOPP, Mylar, Tyvek, and laminate materials at a maximum printing width of 638mm — covering most dry food bags, stand-up pouches, and treat bags.

Resolution and throughput

At 1600 × 1600 dpi and 90–195 ft/min, the Aqua 800M produces legible fine text on large-format panels at volumes suited to sustained flexible packaging production.

ArrowJet Eco 330R for Entry-Level In-House Production

Entry-level capability

The ArrowJet Eco 330R runs on single-phase 230V power with no air compressor needed, producing up to 20 m/min across label and flexible packaging formats at 1600 × 1600 dpi, 324mm max width. See Arrow’s guide to in-house label production for the operational case.

Revision cycle control

Smaller brands lack the volume to negotiate flexible converter minimums. The Eco 330R puts an updated label into production the same day a change is approved.

Frequently Asked Questions — Pet Food Label Design and Printing

Common questions from pet food brand owners, packaging designers, and operations teams.

Where should the guaranteed analysis appear on a pet food label?

Generally on the information panel, formatted as an aligned table separated from the calorie statement and ingredient list — not on the principal display panel. Verify against current AAFCO model regulations and applicable state rules.

What are the AAFCO label requirements for pet food packaging?

AAFCO label requirements generally include product identity, net quantity, guaranteed analysis, ingredient list, nutritional adequacy statement, feeding directions, calorie content, and manufacturer information — each with specific placement rules. Confirm current AAFCO label requirements for your markets before finalizing artwork.

Is a calorie statement always required on pet food labels?

Model regulations generally require a calorie statement expressed as metabolizable energy per kilogram and per a household measure. Format and placement can vary by product type and state — confirm current requirements.

How do functional ingredient claims affect pet food label compliance?

Claims must be truthful, substantiated, and consistent with the formulation and adequacy basis. Disease treatment or prevention claims raise significant regulatory risk. Build claims as modular, independently approvable blocks.

Why is on-demand digital printing useful for pet food brands?

It supports short runs without plate costs, fast versioning, and multi-SKU production for seasonal, regional, and private-label portfolios — reducing obsolete label waste and shortening revision turnaround.

Which ArrowJet press handles cans and bottles vs. flexible bags and pouches?

The ArrowJet Aqua 330R suits pressure-sensitive labels on rigid formats; the ArrowJet Aqua 800M is built for flexible packaging up to 638mm; the ArrowJet Eco 330R provides an entry-level path across both formats up to 324mm.

title.rendered: Tamper-Evident Label Printing: Types, Applications & In-House Options

content.rendered:
Table of Contents

Tamper-Evident Label Printing: Types, Applications & In-House Options

Tamper Evident Label Printing provide visible proof of unauthorized opening — protecting consumers, brands, and supply chains across pharma, food, and personal care.

Quick Answer: Tamper-evident labels are pressure-sensitive labels — or integrated package seals — engineered to show clear physical evidence of opening or interference. Formats include void labels, destructible vinyl, breakaway perforations, and security seals. FDA regulations require tamper-evident packaging for OTC drug products (21 CFR Part 211); requirements for food, cannabis, and personal care vary by jurisdiction. Brands and converters that need short runs, fast revisions, or multi-SKU flexibility can print tamper-evident label stock in-house on digital roll-to-roll presses such as the ArrowJet Aqua 330R and ArrowJet Eco 330R, using tamper-evident facestock supplied on rolls by their substrate vendor.

Key Takeaways

  • Tamper-evident labels show visible evidence of interference — they do not prevent tampering, only reveal it.
  • FDA regulations mandate tamper-evident packaging for OTC drug products; food, cannabis, and personal care requirements vary by jurisdiction and sales channel.
  • Common formats include void labels, destructible vinyl, breakaway seals, and perforated cap bands — each suited to different container shapes and use cases.
  • The right material depends on substrate, storage temperature, container surface energy, and the type of evidence required.
  • Digital in-house printing on tamper-evident facestock eliminates minimum order quantities and enables same-run revisions without plate costs or obsolete pre-printed stock.
  • Arrow sells label printing presses — not label printing services. Brands use Arrow hardware to produce tamper-evident labels on their own production floor.

What Are Tamper-Evident Labels?

Tamper-evident labels are adhesive labels or package seals engineered to reveal visible evidence — a broken pattern, a missing piece, or a surface change — if the package has been opened or disturbed before use.

The term “tamper-evident” is distinct from “tamper-proof.” No label fully prevents a determined person from accessing a product. What tamper-evident labels do is make unauthorized access visible — so consumers, retailers, and brand owners can detect interference before the product is used.

Tamper-evident labels serve five confirmed operational purposes for brands that use them:

  • Protecting consumers from unknowingly using compromised products
  • Reducing manufacturer and retailer liability exposure
  • Supporting brand integrity and consumer confidence at shelf
  • Providing chain-of-custody evidence for recalls and returns investigations
  • Deterring unauthorized opening, refilling, or substitution of contents

This article is general packaging guidance, not legal or regulatory advice. Verify current obligations for your product category and jurisdiction with qualified counsel and your regulatory team before printing.

Why Tamper Evidence Became a Mainstream Requirement

The 1982 Tylenol poisonings were the catalyst that transformed tamper-evident packaging from an optional brand practice into a regulatory expectation for OTC pharmaceuticals.

Before the 1982 incident, over-the-counter medications in the United States were commonly sold without meaningful tamper-evident features. When potassium cyanide-laced capsules were found in Tylenol products on store shelves in the Chicago area, seven people died. The subsequent federal response reshaped packaging law — the FDA moved quickly to require tamper-resistant packaging for OTC drug products, and the broader industry followed.

The food industry, cannabis sector, personal care manufacturers, and electronics brands have since adopted tamper-evident practices for their own product safety, liability, and consumer confidence reasons — extending far beyond pharmaceutical regulation into everyday retail packaging.

Types of Tamper-Evident Label Formats

Four primary tamper-evident label formats cover most packaging applications — each works by a different physical mechanism and suits different container types and use cases.

Format

How It Works

Best For

Considerations

Void Labels

Reveals a “VOID,” “OPENED,” or patterned text on the package surface when the label is removed

Electronics, software, retail goods, warranty seals

Requires a compatible surface; residue remains on package after removal

Destructible Vinyl

Facestock shatters or tears into fragments when peeled — cannot be removed intact

Pharmaceuticals, supplements, cannabis, security seals

Cannot be reprinted at room temperature if laminated; test adhesion on curved surfaces

Breakaway / Cap Seals

Perforated band affixed over a bottle cap or lid tears visibly when the cap is twisted or lifted

Bottles, jars, caps on OTC medications, food condiments

Sizing and perforation placement critical to function; test on actual cap geometry

Perforated Shrink Sleeves

Heat-shrink sleeve wraps the entire container with a perforated tear strip that must be broken to open

Beverages, premium food, personal care, wines and spirits

Requires separate shrink equipment; higher cost per unit than pressure-sensitive labels

Security Seals (Holographic / Sequential)

Serialized or holographic labels used across closures, shipping cartons, or high-value items

High-value retail, supply chain documentation, authentication

Often combined with void features; serialization may require variable data printing

Not every format requires the same printing capability. Void labels and destructible vinyl are pressure-sensitive roll stock — the tamper-evident property is built into the substrate material, not the ink. The label press prints variable data, brand graphics, barcodes, and compliance text onto the tamper-evident facestock using standard inkjet or UV-curable inks.

Industries That Require or Commonly Use Tamper-Evident Labels

Tamper-evident labels are mandatory in some sectors and broadly adopted by practice in others — understanding which obligations apply to your product category is a prerequisite to label specification.

Pharmaceuticals and OTC Medications

FDA regulations under 21 CFR Part 211 require tamper-evident packaging for OTC drug products sold to consumers. Products must use a tamper-evident feature that is distinctive to the product or package, and labeling must include a statement alerting consumers not to use the product if the tamper-evident feature appears to be broken or missing.

Food and Beverage

No single federal rule mandates tamper-evident features for all food products, but FSMA (Food Safety Modernization Act) and retail buyer requirements have pushed broad adoption. Condiments, dressings, pickled products, and premium foods commonly use breakaway seals or induction seals. Foodservice and co-packing contracts frequently specify tamper-evident packaging as a buyer-side requirement.

Cannabis and Hemp Products

State cannabis regulations in most legal markets require child-resistant and tamper-evident packaging for cannabis products sold at retail. Requirements vary significantly by state — California, Colorado, Massachusetts, and others each publish their own specifications. Verify current requirements for each state in which product will be sold before printing.

Dietary Supplements and Nutraceuticals

FDA does not mandate tamper-evident packaging for dietary supplements under the same rules that apply to OTC drugs, but GMP guidelines under 21 CFR Part 111 require controls over product integrity, and many retailers and distributors require tamper-evident features as a supplier qualification condition. Consumer expectation in the supplement category strongly favors tamper evidence.

Personal Care and Cosmetics

No federal tamper-evident mandate applies specifically to personal care or cosmetic products under MoCRA (Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022). However, brands in the personal care space widely use breakaway seals and void labels for brand protection and retail shrink reduction, particularly on higher-margin SKUs.

Electronics and High-Value Consumer Goods

Warranty void seals are common on electronics to detect unauthorized disassembly before warranty claims. These are typically void-pattern pressure-sensitive labels applied over screws, seams, or battery compartments. The tamper-evidence function here is brand protection and warranty administration rather than consumer safety.

Regulatory Overview by Product Category

No single regulation governs tamper-evident packaging across all product categories — requirements differ by agency, product type, and sales channel.

Product Category

Primary Regulatory Framework

Tamper-Evident Status

OTC Drug Products

FDA — 21 CFR Part 211.132

Mandatory for retail products accessible to consumers

Food Products

FDA — FSMA; retail buyer specs vary

Not universally mandated; broadly adopted by practice and buyer requirement

Dietary Supplements

FDA — 21 CFR Part 111 (GMP); retailer requirements

Not federally mandated; widely required by retailers and distributors

Cannabis Products

State-level regulation (varies by state)

Required in most legal retail cannabis markets; specifications vary by state

Personal Care / Cosmetics

FDA — MoCRA (2022); no specific tamper-evident rule

Not federally mandated; commonly adopted for brand protection

Electronics / Consumer Goods

No applicable federal tamper-evident regulation

Voluntary; used for warranty and brand protection purposes

This table is a general reference only. Regulatory requirements change. Verify current obligations with qualified legal counsel and your regulatory team before committing to a label specification or production run.

Printing Tamper-Evident Labels In-House

Brands that print tamper-evident labels in-house on digital label presses gain same-day revision capability and eliminate minimum order quantities — two operational advantages that matter most when formulas or regulations change.

The tamper-evident property of void, destructible vinyl, and security seal labels is built into the facestock material — not applied by the printer. Tamper-evident label stock is available on rolls from specialist substrate suppliers and prints on the same roll-to-roll digital presses used for standard pressure-sensitive labels. The press applies brand graphics, variable data, barcodes, compliance text, and lot codes onto the pre-engineered tamper-evident substrate.

Two operational models exist for in-house tamper-evident label production:

High-Volume In-House Label Production

Operations running multiple label SKUs, frequent regulatory revisions, or compliance-driven reprints benefit from a production-grade roll-to-roll press. The ArrowJet Aqua 330R is a high-speed single-pass aqueous pigment press printing at up to 150 ft/min (45.7 m/min) at 1600 × 1600 dpi, with a 12.75″ (324 mm) max print width. It handles standard label substrates including BOPP, PET, and specialty security stocks, and supports a bulk 10L ink system for extended production runs.

For pharmaceutical, supplement, or food brands managing a large label portfolio with GMP version control requirements, in-house printing on a press like the Aqua 330R Lite provides traceability: each print run is executed from the current approved file, eliminating the risk of applying pre-printed labels that are no longer current.

Entry-Level In-House Label Production

Converters and brand operations scaling up from desktop printers — or those bringing label production in-house for the first time — can enter digital label printing at lower capital and operating cost. The ArrowJet Eco 330R is a compact industrial single-pass press running at up to 20 m/min with 1600 × 1600 dpi resolution, 324 mm max print width, single-phase power (no air compressor required), and a footprint that fits production environments where space is limited. It handles CMYK water-based pigment inks on the same roll-format tamper-evident substrates used on larger presses.

For operations producing a moderate volume of tamper-evident labels across a manageable SKU count, the Eco 330R offers production-grade output without the infrastructure requirements of a larger press.

Matching the Right Format to the Right Package

No single tamper-evident format works for every container — the correct choice depends on container shape, surface energy, closure geometry, storage conditions, and the type of evidence required.

Before committing to a label specification or placing a production order, test the chosen label or seal on the actual packaging substrate under production and storage conditions. Confirm that it:

  • Adheres properly to the container material and geometry (curved bottles, flat cartons, and irregular shapes each behave differently)
  • Reveals tampering as intended under normal handling — and does not trigger false-positive evidence from ordinary stacking, shipping vibration, or temperature change
  • Does not interfere with normal customer opening — excessive difficulty opening a legitimate seal creates user experience problems without security benefit
  • Remains legible after adhesion — barcodes, lot codes, and expiration dates printed on the label must scan and read cleanly after application

Material selection follows from these requirements. Destructible vinyl adheres best to smooth, relatively flat surfaces and is well suited to capsule bottles, flat-panel closures, and secondary seals on boxes. Void labels require a substrate with sufficient surface energy to retain the transfer layer when the label is removed — test on the actual container material. Breakaway cap seals require precise sizing to the cap diameter and torque profile; off-the-shelf sizing rarely works without fitment verification.

Tamper-evident labels are a packaging tool — not a guarantee of product safety, authenticity, or legal compliance. Use them as part of a broader packaging and quality system, and confirm all applicable regulatory requirements before production.

Frequently Asked Questions — Tamper-Evident Labels

What does tamper-evident mean on a label?

A tamper-evident label includes a physical feature designed to show visible evidence if the package has been opened, altered, or disturbed before it reaches the end user. Common mechanisms include void patterns revealed on removal, destructible vinyl that cannot be peeled intact, and breakaway perforations that cannot be resealed.

Are tamper-evident labels required by law?

Requirements vary by product category and jurisdiction. OTC drug products in the United States are subject to FDA tamper-evident packaging regulations under 21 CFR Part 211.132. Food, cannabis, and personal care products face different — and sometimes overlapping — obligations depending on the sales channel, state, and federal rules in effect. Verify current obligations for your specific product category with qualified legal counsel before printing.

What types of tamper-evident labels are most common?

The most common formats are void labels (which reveal a “VOID” or “OPENED” pattern on removal), destructible vinyl seals (which shatter when peeled), breakaway cap seals (which tear at a perforation when the cap is twisted), and full-body shrink sleeves with perforations. The right format depends on container shape, substrate, storage conditions, and product category requirements.

Can brands print tamper-evident labels in-house?

Yes. Digital roll-to-roll label presses such as the ArrowJet Aqua 330R and the ArrowJet Eco 330R print on tamper-evident facestock substrates — including destructible vinyl, void material, and security seal stock — supplied on rolls by substrate vendors. In-house printing eliminates minimum order quantities, reduces revision turnaround from weeks to hours, and removes the risk of applying outdated pre-printed labels when formulas or regulations change.

What label materials are used for tamper-evident printing?

Common tamper-evident facestock materials include destructible vinyl (shatters when peeled), void polyester (reveals a hidden pattern on removal), ultra-removable adhesive films (adheres strongly to the container but releases cleanly from the label face), and high-tack polypropylene with tear-at-opening perforations. Material selection depends on container surface, storage temperature, and the type of evidence the label is intended to provide.

Which industries require or commonly use tamper-evident labels?

Tamper-evident labels are standard in pharmaceuticals and OTC medications (FDA-regulated), food and beverage (retail and foodservice), dietary supplements and nutraceuticals, cannabis and hemp products (state-regulated), personal care and cosmetics, and electronics or high-value consumer goods. Each industry applies different specifications and regulatory frameworks.

Arrow Systems manufactures digital label presses used by pharmaceutical, food, supplement, and consumer goods brands to print tamper-evident labels on-demand — no plates, no minimums, no obsolete pre-printed inventory. The ArrowJet Aqua 330R and the ArrowJet Eco 330R are available for evaluation with sample print runs on your own substrate.
